text:
Let the two liquids in the starting equimolar mixture X be A and B.

1.  Both A and B decolorise Br₂-water  ⇒  each contains C=C (not aromatic).
2.  After heating with Pt they undergo a self-disproportionation to give an equimolar mixture Y of two liquids that no longer decolorise Br₂-water.
   • One component of Y must be the hydrocarbon Z ( because Z is said to be a constituent of Y and is obtained on hydrogenation of Y).  
   • Z does not add more H₂ and has H-mass % = 14.28 %.  
     For a hydrocarbon CₙH₂ₙ the H-mass fraction is  

         2n·1 / (12n + 2n) = 2 / 14 = 0.1428 = 14.28 %

     Thus Z has the general formula CₙH₂ₙ : a saturated (no further H₂ uptake) ring alkane.  
     The most familiar solvent fitting this description is cyclohexane, C₆H₁₂.

3.  The other component of Y must also fail to decolorise Br₂-water.  
   Benzene (C₆H₆) fulfils this (it is aromatic and does not add Br₂ without a catalyst).  
   Moreover, on vigorous hydrogenation benzene gives cyclohexane, so hydrogenating Y (cyclohexane + benzene) yields only cyclohexane, exactly as stated.

4.  Work backwards to mixture X.  
   In a Pt-catalysed “disproportionation (transfer-hydrogenation)” reaction two cyclohexanoid molecules can interchange hydrogen:

        C₆H₁₀  +  C₆H₈   ⟶   C₆H₁₂  +  C₆H₆
       cyclohexene   1,4-cyclohexadiene   cyclohexane   benzene

   • Cyclohexene (C₆H₁₀) and 1,4-cyclohexadiene (C₆H₈) are both non-conjugated alkenes, they decolorise Br₂-water, and each hydrogenates to cyclohexane, giving the observed result for mixture X.

5.  Total number of H atoms in the two liquids of mixture X:

        Cyclohexene      : C₆H₁₀  → 10 H
        1,4-Cyclohexadiene: C₆H₈   →  8 H
        Total H atoms = 10 + 8 = 18

Hence the correct total number of hydrogen atoms is 18.

Answer: B
